title: Knudsen forgetful morphism as the universal stable curve
statement: Let $S$ be a scheme, $g\geq2$ and $r\geq0$. Use the stable ordered pointed moduli groupoids [def-sfb-stable-pointed-moduli-groupoids]. There is a natural forgetful-and-stabilizing morphism $F_r:\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,r+1}\to\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,r}$. For every stable ordered $r$-pointed family $(X\to T,s_1,\ldots,s_r)$, the 2-fibre product $T\times_{\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,r}}\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,r+1}$ is represented by the total scheme $X$, over $T$. Under this identification a point of $X$ is an additional arbitrary section of $X$, and the corresponding $(r+1)$-pointed family is obtained by stabilization: a rational component is inserted if the extra section meets a marking or node. Contraction after forgetting the last marking and stabilization are mutually inverse, naturally under arbitrary base change. Consequently the base change of $F_r$ to any scheme is a projective flat finitely presented curve, with projectivity in [def-trf-projective-bundle-morphism]. On the open subcategory where the family is smooth and the new section is disjoint from the old sections, stabilization is the identity on the underlying curve and simply appends that section. Stable ordered pointed families in this convention remain stable after arbitrary base change. Families and isomorphisms in this assertion use exactly the ordered-label convention in the definition. Schemes, fibre products, flatness and finite presentation use [def-pc-scheme], [def-pc-fibre-product], [def-weil-flat-morphism] and [def-sbc-locally-finite-presentation].

source.place: Section 2, contraction and stabilization, especially Corollary 2.6 and Theorem 2.7, printed pp.178--180. Local PDF WANTED; publisher PDF and indexed primary-author scan consulted online.

proof.text: First check the convention under pullback $T'\to T$. A stable family is proper by the projective-bundle properness lemma, and its pullback is proper by proper base change. Regard the disjoint sections as their disjoint union: the semistable marked base-change lemma gives flatness, finite presentation, nodality and disjoint smooth sections after pullback. For every algebraically closed $\Omega$ and $\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to T'$, its geometric fibre is the original fibre for the composite to $T$. Thus connectedness, genus and every component's stability inequality are literally the same. Apply the log-canonical algebra lemma to the pulled-back proper family: its degrees are all positive (genus zero has at least three special points, genus one at least one, and genus at least two has positive degree). Its no-zero-component clause identifies the family with the stated relative Proj and supplies projective-bundle projectivity. This verifies stability after arbitrary base change without changing projectivity conventions.

source.place: Section 1 and Proposition 2.1; arbitrary geometric-point definition of stability.

proof.text: Given a stable $(r+1)$-pointed family $Y$, retain only its first $r$ markings in $D$. In the degree formula for $\omega_Y(D)$ the component containing the last marking loses exactly one special point. All other degrees stay positive. A rational component can reach zero only if it had exactly three special points, one the last marking. Such a component is smooth: if it had a self-node, its two remaining special points would be the two branches of that self-node, so it would meet no other component and would be the whole connected fibre, of arithmetic genus $1$, contradicting $g\geq2$. A genus-one component could reach zero only if its sole special point was the last marking; it would then have no attaching branch, hence would be the entire connected fibre, contradicting $g\geq2$. Components of larger genus keep positive degree. Thus the hypotheses of the log-canonical algebra lemma hold, with at most one zero component. Its evaluation contraction $q:Y\to X$ gives a stable ordered $r$-pointed family and an arbitrary section $\Delta=q t$. This is functorial in isomorphisms and arbitrary base change. Call this functor $c$; discarding $\Delta$ defines the required $F_r$. For an arrow over $u:T\prime\to T$, apply $c$ to its labelled pullback isomorphism and use the canonical base-change comparison for $q$. This gives the required arrow over $u$; naturality and uniqueness of the contraction comparison respect identities and the fibre-product associativity used in composition.

Conversely start with a stable $r$-pointed $X$ and arbitrary section $\Delta$. Properness follows from its projective-bundle presentation. Form exactly the module $\mathcal K$ and expansion $Z=\operatorname{Proj}_X\operatorname{Sym}\mathcal K$ of the section-ideal lemma. That lemma gives a proper flat finitely presented nodal family with the disjoint ordered lifts. Its fibre description proves stability: an inserted tail has its old marking, new marking and attachment; an inserted bridge has its new marking and two attachments. Each has three special points. On every old component a lost marking or branch is replaced by an attachment, so its old stability inequality is unchanged. Genus remains $g$. The log-canonical lemma in its positive-degree case supplies projective-bundle projectivity of $Z\to T$. These constructions define a functor $s$ to stable $(r+1)$-pointed families, compatible with all base changes and all labelled isomorphisms.

source.place: Definition 2.3 and Theorem 2.4; projectivity from the logarithmic algebra.

proof.text: For $p:s(X,\Delta)\to X$, the fibre description shows that the only component that becomes degree zero after deleting the new marking is the inserted tail or bridge; $p$ contracts exactly that component. If none was inserted the fibre map is an isomorphism. The uniqueness clause of the log-canonical contraction therefore identifies $c(s(X,\Delta))$ with $(X,\Delta)$, preserving every old section and the image of the new one. The identification is canonical and respects base change.

For the contraction $q:Y\to X$ from step 2, put $\Delta=q t$. The evaluation lemma applies: its exceptional component has the last marking and exactly two old special points. It gives the quotient $q^*\mathcal K\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal O_Y(t)\otimes q^*\mathcal O_X(D)$. The projective-bundle quotient theorem gives an $X$-map $f:Y\to s(X,\Delta)$ preserving all ordered markings. Its geometric fibre maps are isomorphisms: by the evaluation lemma $f$ is the identity off the exceptional component and maps that component onto the inserted projective line by its complete degree-one linear system, and by the fibre description of the section-ideal expansion the fibre of $s(X,\Delta)$ is exactly the fibre of $X$ with that line inserted at $\Delta$ (or unchanged when $q$ is a fibrewise isomorphism). Apply the universal-isomorphism-open lemma to the two structural maps to $T$: the source is flat and finitely presented and proper, the target is proper and hence separated, closed and locally of finite type. Its representing open contains every geometric point, so equals $T$, and $f$ is an isomorphism. Evaluation and the quotient classification make $f$ natural in all isomorphisms of contraction diagrams and arbitrary base changes. In particular an automorphism $h$ over the identity of $(X,\Delta)$ satisfies $fh=f$; as $f$ is an isomorphism, $h=1$. This also gives uniqueness of an arrow between two objects over a fixed $(X,\Delta)$.

source.place: Lemma 2.5 and Corollary 2.6; Stacks Tag 05XD for the relative isomorphism test.

proof.text: Over $U\to T$, the defined 2-fibre product has an object $Y$ with $\phi:X_U\xrightarrow{\sim}F_r(Y)$ preserving every old label. Set $\alpha=\phi^{-1}$. Send this object to the section $\alpha(qt)$ of $X_U$. An arrow $h:Y\to Y\prime$ satisfies $F_r(h)\phi=\phi\prime$, equivalently $\alpha\prime F_r(h)=\alpha$, so the section is unchanged. Reverse this assignment by applying $s$ to $X_U$ and that section, equipped with the inverse of the comparison in step 4. Steps 4 and 5 identify both composites with the identity. For two objects giving the same section, their comparisons in step 5 give an arrow between them over $X_U$; its uniqueness follows from the automorphism calculation there. Thus the equivalence is to the discrete groupoid of sections of $X_U\to U$. By the fibre-product universal property, those sections are exactly $T$-maps $U\to X$. Naturality of contraction, expansion and their comparisons respects pullback $U\prime\to U$ and canonical fibre-product associativity, giving the claimed representation over schemes. Its structural morphism is projective, flat and finitely presented by the original stable-family definition. The isomorphism $\phi$ remains part of each object; the old labels are preserved individually.

source.place: Corollary 2.6, unwinding the 2-fibre product and its arrows; previous comparisons in steps 4--5.

proof.text: On the required open subcategory, the extra section is smooth and disjoint from every old marking. The fibre description of the section-ideal expansion says that its projection $p:Z\to X$ is an isomorphism on every geometric fibre. Apply the universal-isomorphism-open lemma with base $T$, source $Z$ and target $X$: both structural morphisms are proper, flat and finitely presented, so all its hypotheses hold. Its open contains every geometric point and hence equals $T$. Thus $p$ itself is an isomorphism. Since the canonical lifted sections map to the old sections and to $\Delta$, this identifies the stabilization, including all labels, with the original curve with $\Delta$ appended. The canonical projection and its inverse respect every base change.
